quote: The color that cowardice brought to my face
note: Dante has gone pale with fear at seeing Virgil shut out of the gate (Canto 8). Virgil, seeing it, hides his own alarm so as not to frighten him more.

quote: She who offered herself to us
note: Virgil starts to doubt aloud ("Otherwise...") and stops himself. The one who offered help is usually taken to be Beatrice, who came down to Limbo and promised Heaven's support for the journey (Inferno 2). Dante's Italian is vaguer: "such a one offered".
"Otherwise..." Dante finishes it for himself: otherwise we are lost.
A tactful way of asking a frightening question: has Virgil ever been down here, and does he really know the way?

context: Virgil's own circle. Dante sums up its punishment in three words: hope cut away.
The story that she once sent Virgil to the bottom of Hell is found nowhere before Dante. He seems to have invented it so that his guide can know the road.

note: The wall of Dis, the one now barred against them.
Judecca, the last zone of the ninth circle, at the very bottom of Hell. It is named for Judas, who betrayed Christ, and holds those who betrayed their lords and benefactors (Inferno 34).
The outermost of the turning heavens, which wraps around all the others and carries them with it. The center of the earth, where Judas is, is the point of the universe farthest from it.
The Italian says "without anger". Some read it as the righteous anger the poets will need, others as the anger of the devils who resist them.

context: They appear on the tower above the gate, tearing at themselves. In the allegory they are often read as the torment of a guilty conscience, remorse that brings no repentance.

note: Hydras are water snakes, worn here as belts. The horned vipers of the next line are cerastes, desert snakes with a small horn over each eye. The details come from the Furies of Latin poetry, in Virgil, Ovid and Statius.

context: The Furies are her handmaids. Virgil, who wrote about them, knows them at sight.

note: The three names come from the Latin poets. In the Aeneid, Alecto is sent up from the underworld to stir Italy to war, and Tisiphone, in a bloodstained robe, keeps sleepless watch at the gate of Tartarus.

context: She never appears. What she stands for is much debated: most often despair, which hardens the heart so that a sinner can no longer turn back, or the doubt and unbelief of the heretics just inside the wall.
He came down alive to help a friend carry off Proserpina, and was caught. In the version Dante follows, Hercules freed him. The Furies regret it: one living man got away, and now here is another.

note: Medusa. One look at her face turned the living to stone.

quote: shielding my eyes with his own
note: Dante's Italian has Virgil cover Dante's eyes with his own hands, on top of Dante's. Reason does what it can to keep the danger out of sight, but it cannot open the gate.

quote: O you who have clear understanding
note: One of the poem's famous addresses to the reader, and its plainest statement that the story carries a hidden meaning. Dante doesn't say what the meaning is, or whether he means the Furies and Medusa or the rescue that follows. Readers have argued about it for seven centuries.
Medieval science, following Aristotle, held that strong winds arise where hot and cold air meet.
The scummy surface of the marsh, as old as Hell.
The simile recalls Ovid's story of the peasants turned into frogs, who dive into the mud of their pond. The damned are the frogs, and the one who comes is their enemy.

The messenger Virgil was waiting for. Dante never names him. Nearly all commentators take him for an angel, and he comes like Christ at the Harrowing of Hell, before whom the gates could not stand. He walks on the water as Christ did on the Sea of Galilee.
Hell has no power over him. Its foul air is only a nuisance, to be waved away.
A sign of authority, like a herald's staff or a scepter. A touch is enough. Some readers think of the wand of Mercury, the messenger of the gods in classical poetry.
The devils, who were angels until they rebelled with Lucifer and were thrown down.
An echo of the voice that stops Saul on the road to Damascus: "It is hard for you to kick against the goads" (Acts 26:14). The will is God's.

context: For his last labor, Hercules dragged Cerberus up to the daylight on a chain, which scraped his neck raw. The angel's point: you resisted a higher will before, and it only hurt you.

note: He has done his errand and thinks only of going back. The blessed take no interest in Hell.
A city in Provence near the mouth of the Rhône, with a famous Roman and early Christian cemetery, the Alyscamps. Its stone tombs covered a wide field outside the walls.

Pula, at the tip of the Istrian peninsula in present-day Croatia, where an ancient burial ground once lay outside the town. The Quarnaro is the gulf beside it, which Dante counts as Italy's eastern border.

quote: All their lids were lifted up
note: The tombs stand open for now. Canto 10 says when they will be shut.

The sixth circle, just inside the wall. Dante's word is eresiarchi, the founders and leaders of heresies. In his time convicted heretics were burned, and here they burn forever. Heresy is a sin of belief, so it fits neither the sins of weakness above nor the sins of violence and fraud below.
Each tomb holds the followers of one heresy, and the worse the error, the hotter the tomb.
In Hell the poets nearly always turn left as they circle downward. They turn right only here and once more, in Inferno 17. No one has explained it for certain.
